_note: Build Your Own Rover. An EDUCATIONAL SIMULATION with fictional missions and illustrative numbers (budget points, mass units, power units). It is not a real engineering tool. The 'Real-world reference' notes are the only factual statements; each links to a NASA source already used in this project (docs/research-sources.md).

missions.name: Shadow Crater Survey
missions.brief: A fictional mission to drive into a cold crater floor that never sees sunlight, and press a spectrometer against the soil to look for clues that ice might be mixed into it.
notes: There is almost no sunlight on the crater floor, so solar power struggles.
Slopes into the crater are steep and rough.

missions.name: Ancient Water Detective
missions.brief: A fictional mission to cross several kilometres of plains to layered rock outcrops, and find out whether those rocks formed in water.
notes: Composition and grain-scale texture are the key evidence, so instruments must touch the rock.
Long drives over soft ground: getting stuck is a real risk.

missions.name: Dust and Sky Watch
missions.brief: A fictional mission to stay at one site for a long time, watching dust, clouds and how the surface changes through the seasons.
notes: Dust will settle on everything over months, including solar panels.
Lots of images and measurements to send home.

options.name: 4 small wheels
options.desc: Light and cheap, but struggles on rough or soft ground.

options.name: 6 wheels with flexible suspension
options.desc: Keeps all wheels on uneven ground. A good all-rounder.

options.name: 6 large wheels, heavy-duty
options.desc: Climbs and crosses soft ground best, but is heavy and costly.

options.name: Navigation cameras only
options.desc: Enough to drive safely. Little science detail.

options.name: Panoramic colour stereo camera on a mast
options.desc: Wide colour views for choosing targets and studying the landscape.

options.name: Spectrometer
options.desc: Measures which elements and minerals are present. Placed against the target.

options.name: Microscopic imager
options.desc: Close-up views of grain size and texture.

options.name: Rock abrasion tool
options.desc: Grinds away a rock's dusty outer surface so instruments can see fresh rock.

options.name: Magnet targets
options.desc: Collects magnetic dust so cameras can study it.

options.name: Weather station
options.desc: Measures temperature, wind and pressure over time.

options.name: No arm
options.desc: Saves budget, but contact instruments cannot reach a rock.

options.name: Arm with an instrument turret
options.desc: Places contact instruments on rocks and soil.

options.name: Small solar panels
options.desc: Cheap and light. Output drops with less sunlight or dust on the panels.

options.name: Large solar panels
options.desc: More power in sunlight, but still depends on the Sun and clean panels.

options.name: Radioisotope power source
options.desc: Steady power day and night, whatever the dust. Very expensive in this simulation.

options.name: Direct-to-Earth antenna
options.desc: Talks straight to Earth. Simple, but sends data slowly.

options.name: Orbiter relay radio
options.desc: Sends data through a spacecraft in orbit: more data per day.

options.name: Both, for backup
options.desc: More data and a backup if one link fails.

references.text: Spirit and Opportunity were solar-powered rovers that carried a panoramic camera, an Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometer, a Mössbauer spectrometer, a Microscopic Imager, a Rock Abrasion Tool and a magnet array.
Spirit broke through a thin crust into soft sand in 2009 and got stuck. Its solar panels then could not gather enough sunlight to survive the winter.
Opportunity, also solar-powered, last communicated on 10 June 2018, while a planet-wide dust storm blanketed its location.
Over four years, dust slowly covered InSight's solar panels. Its dusty panels produced less power until the mission ended in December 2022.
Phoenix, a solar-powered lander, was not designed to survive the dark and cold conditions of a Martian arctic winter.
Viking 1's sampler arm carried a magnet, and studying the magnetic properties of the Martian surface was one of the lander's goals.

disclaimer: Build Your Own Rover is an educational simulation. The missions are fictional and every cost, mass and power number is illustrative. It is not a real engineering design tool. Real-world reference notes link to NASA sources.
